Diverse legal case retrieval using submodular optimization

A controlled study of when choosing search results as a set, rather than ranking them one by one, helps a lawyer see every issue in a case.

01 · PROBLEM

Rankings repeat themselves

Search engines such as TF-IDF and BM25 score every case on its own and return the top few. If one topic scores high, all its look-alikes score high too and fill the list. A lawyer whose dispute involves late payment, wrongful termination and an unfair penalty clause may see seven late-payment cases while the other two issues sit at rank 30 to 60.

Redundancy

Near-duplicate cases consume result slots without adding information.

Missing issues

Relevant cases on secondary issues are pushed below the cut-off.

Misleading metrics

Precision alone cannot see either problem, so diversity metrics are needed too.

02 · METHOD

Select a set that covers the ground

BM25 first shortlists a pool of about 100 cases. Greedy selection then builds a set of 10 one case at a time, always adding the case that raises the objective most. The objective has diminishing returns (it is submodular), so a case similar to one already chosen adds little.

F(S) = (1 − λ) · (1/k) Σ r(s) + λ · Σⱼ rⱼ · maxs∈S sim(j, s) / Σⱼ rⱼ

Relevance term

Normalised BM25 score of each chosen case against the query.

Coverage term

Facility-location function: how well the set represents the whole pool, using cosine similarity of TF-IDF vectors.

The λ dial

λ = 0 reproduces BM25. λ = 1 ignores the query score. Values between trade relevance for variety.

Greedy reaches at least 63% of the best possible set for this class of function (Nemhauser, Wolsey and Fisher, 1978). The IR Lab checks the real ratio against brute force.

07 · SCOPE AND LIMITS

Read before trusting the numbers

Synthetic text

Cases are random words from issue vocabularies. Results show when the method can help, not that it works on real courts.

Shared bias

The generator and retrievers both think in bags of words. An LLM-rewritten subset and single-issue controls test for this.

Pool ceiling

A relevant case outside the BM25 pool can never be recovered by selection.

Not a new algorithm

The contribution is a careful study of when set selection beats ranking, including where it fails.

      Read this before trusting any number

      • The corpus is synthetic word soup. These results show when the method can help, not that it works on real courts.
      • The generator and BM25 both think in bags of words, which may flatter the method. The full study checks this with LLM-rewritten text and negative controls.
      • Pick the single-issue queries to see a negative control: variety should give no gain there.
      • If a relevant case is not in the BM25 pool, set selection can never recover it. Shrink the pool to see this.
      • This page runs the core of E1, E3 and E8. MAP, NDCG, α-NDCG, the exact-optimum check (E6), the dense and hybrid grid (E10) and the regression (E9) belong to the full Python study.

      Python pipeline, stage by stage

      Everything on this tab was produced by the Python package legal_retrieval_py and exported with export_frontend.py. A web page cannot run Python itself, so these are the real outputs of one recorded run (seed 0, 30% near-copies, k = 10, pool = 100, λ = 0.7), not live computation. The other tabs run the same method in JavaScript.

      Full experiment run (10 seeds)

      Key findings
      • BM25 top 10 covers about 49% of query issues on multi-issue queries; submodular selection covers about 86% with far fewer near-copies.
      • MMR scored higher than submodular on S-recall and α-NDCG at λ = 0.7, so "submodular beats MMR" is not supported by this data.
      • On single-issue controls, submodular was neutral in all 60 runs.
      • Greedy reached at least 0.999 of the exact optimum on small pools; lazy greedy used about a quarter of the evaluations.
      • Hybrid-pool failure explained (E12): the pool holds the same issues, but its relevance scores are nearly flat, so λ = 0.7 under-weights coverage. At λ ≥ 0.9 it recovers (S-recall 0.88 to 0.98). A cross-validated ridge model that learns λ per query reached α-NDCG 0.646 against 0.513 for fixed λ = 0.7.
      • Even with bootstrap intervals, MMR beats submodular on α-NDCG (difference −0.18, 95% interval −0.21 to −0.16). Submodular beats BM25 and xQuAD.

      Run it yourself: pip install -r requirements.txt, then python run_experiments.py --seeds 10 --out results, then python export_frontend.py.

      About this data

      100 full Supreme Court of India judgments, mostly from the 1950s to 1990s, taken from the public GitHub repository sassysohom48/JusticeRAG (code under the MIT licence). That repository does not state where the judgment texts came from, so confirm the source and terms before publishing results. For a final version, the Indian Supreme Court Judgments dataset on AWS Open Data (CC-BY-4.0) is a documented source.

      Topic labels are assigned automatically by keyword rules, not by lawyers, and the LLM can be wrong. Treat matches as leads to read, not as advice.
